method_card.title: Estimating Gradients of Curves & Areas Under Graphs
steps: Gradient at a point: draw the tangent, then rise ÷ run.
Area: use the trapezium rule, A ≈ (h ÷ 2)[first + last + 2(middles)].
Speed-time area = distance; distance-time gradient = speed.
Keep the ½ and double only the inside y-values.
method_card.content:
The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent there (rise ÷ run). The area under a curve is estimated with the trapezium rule:

$$A \approx \frac{h}{2}\left[y_0 + y_n + 2(y_1 + \ldots + y_{n-1})\right]$$

where h is the strip width. On a speed-time graph the area is the distance; on a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed.
method_card.example:
Estimate the area under \(y = x^2\) from 0 to 4, 4 strips (h = 1). y-values 0, 1, 4, 9, 16.

$$A \approx \tfrac{1}{2}[0 + 16 + 2(1 + 4 + 9)] = \tfrac{1}{2}(44) = 22$$

guided_steps.hint: Second y take away the first y.
Second x take away the first x.

guided_steps.say: Now divide the rise by the run.
guided_steps.hint: Rise on top, run underneath.

guided_steps.done: It lands on (5, 11), so the gradient is 2.
guided_steps.hint: Add the rise back on; you should reach the second point's y.

bronze.hint: Area of the rectangle is width times height, and that area is the distance.

misconceptions.message: Add is not the operation here. Area = width × height = 5 × 12 = 60 m.

guided_steps.say: On a speed-time graph the distance is the area of the shape. This is a rectangle: width × height.

guided_steps.done: Distance ÷ time returns the steady speed 12 m/s, so the distance is 60 m.

silver.display: Use the trapezium rule with 3 strips (\(h = 2\)) and y-values 0, 4, 12, 24 to estimate the area.
silver.hint: Double the middle values, add the ends, then multiply by h over 2.

misconceptions.message: You have left out the ½ in h ÷ 2. Multiply the bracket by h ÷ 2 = 1, not by h = 2. The answer is 56, not 112.
The middle values 4 and 12 must be doubled. With them counted once you get (2 ÷ 2)(0 + 24 + 16) = 40; doubled it is 56.

guided_steps.say: Trapezium rule: A = (h ÷ 2) × [first + last + 2 × (all the middle values)].

guided_steps.hint: Every y-value except the first and last.
The inside values all count twice.
Only the two end values, each once.
Add the ends to the doubled middles.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply by h ÷ 2 to finish.

Multiply the half-width by the bracket.

gold.display: Explain why using more strips in the trapezium rule gives a better estimate. What happens to the accuracy as the number of strips increases?
options: Accuracy increases, strips better approximate the curve
No change, it is always exact
Accuracy depends on the curve shape only
gold.hint: Think about how well a narrow straight-topped strip matches a curve compared with a wide one.

misconceptions.message: More strips means each strip is narrower, so its straight top hugs the curve more closely. The estimate gets better, not worse.

bronze.title: Bronze: gradient by rise over run, and simple areas
steps: Gradient of a straight tangent = rise ÷ run. Pick two clear points; rise is the change in y, run is the change in x.
Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height. Trapezium = ½ × (a + b) × height. Rectangle = width × height.
On a speed-time graph the area is the distance; on a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed.

example.question: A tangent passes through (1, 2) and (4, 8). Find its gradient.

silver.title: Silver: the trapezium rule
steps: Split the area into equal strips of width h (h = total width ÷ number of strips).
Read the y-values in order; double only the inside ones, and keep the ½ in h ÷ 2.

gold.title: Gold: harder strips and interpretation
steps: Decimal strip widths and y-values work the same way: keep h ÷ 2 exact.
More strips means narrower strips, so the estimate fits the curve more closely and improves.
For a curve bending upward the trapeziums lie above it, so the rule overestimates.

steps.say: You just found a distance by taking the area under a speed-time graph. When the graph is a neat rectangle it is easy. When it curves, we chop the area into thin strips and add them (the trapezium rule). And the steepness of a graph at a point has meaning too: on a distance-time graph the gradient of the tangent is the speed right then.
